title: Planetary boundaries
what: Why the boundaries sit where they do: global temperature over 800,000 years, through the ice ages to the narrow band it kept for the 10,000 years before industry, the Holocene corridor, and out of it. Then the nine Earth-system processes that keep the planet in a Holocene-like state, each with a boundary to human pressure, and where each control variable stood in the Planetary Health Check 2026: inside its safe operating space, in the zone of increasing risk, or in the high-risk zone. Beside it, the assessment the report compares itself with, Richardson et al. (2023).
how: The temperature chart is this site's own drawing of the four records the report's Figure 1 cites, fetched and checked by the data pipeline: the EPICA Dome C ice core (Antarctic, thinned to 200- and 1,000-year means), the Last Glacial Maximum Reanalysis (median and 95% range of 500 members), PAGES 2k (31-year filtered ensemble) and HadCRUT5 (annual, the latest, perhaps partial, year left out). The global records are set against 1850–1900; the corridor is the range of the reanalysis' medians over the 10,000 years before 1950, computed, not drawn. The values are the report's Table 7.1, typed by hand, for both assessments; each boundary's status in words is the report's own, and the site checks that its drawing agrees with every one. Each wedge reaches from the variable's reference value (0) through its boundary (1) to its high-risk line (2), beyond that eased so the strongest transgressions stay in view; each assessment is drawn against its own boundaries. Ranges (extinction rates, HANPP) and judgements (novel entities, with no numbers past its boundary) are drawn faded past their sure part. The 2023 values are taken as the 2026 report reprints them. The scene and its colours are this site's own, after the report's description of its diagrams. While the Holocene chapter's chart draws, the globe follows it: the ice sheets (PaleoMIST, with Batchelor et al.'s outlines), the coast at the sea level of the time (Bintanja & van de Wal, on NOAA's present-day depths), the sea ice (blended from NSIDC's today towards a PMIP4 model's glacial maximum) and, on land, Krapp et al.'s temperature as the change from today; from 1850, Berkeley Earth's measured temperature of land and sea (the sea's surface water, from HadSST4; the air over sea ice) as 5-year means against 1850–1900. Where a place had too few records in 1850–1900 (about a third of the land, much of it tropical, and two fifths of the sea, away from the ships' tracks), its warming is measured from 1951–1980 and shifted back by how much warmer 1951–1980 was than 1850–1900 in its 15° band of latitude, land and sea apart: some 0.3 to 0.6 °C on land, 0.05 to 0.4 °C at sea. That shift is estimated, the warming since is measured. Inland Antarctica, without records that long, is left plain, as is the sea where the early years have too few records.
others: The ice core is Antarctic temperature, which swings about twice as far as the globe's: it is drawn faint and named, not rescaled. Records disagree on the Holocene's slow trend: the reanalysis drawn (Osman et al. 2021) has it warming gently, where others have it peaking some 6,000 years ago and cooling; the corridor holds either way. Where the two assessments differ, the site shows both rather than choose. Global phosphorus: the 2026 table gives 4.4 Tg/yr, inside the boundary, where 2023 gave 22.6, yet the report's text still calls both nutrient boundaries strongly transgressed and lists no new data for them. Forest cover rose from 60% to 64%, and its boundary from 75% to 78%, through a corrected method, the report says, not forest recovering. Ocean acidification crossed its boundary for the first time in 2026, by a hair (Ω 2.85 against 2.86), with four data products where 2023 had one. Aerosols over South Asia are measured against a boundary proposed in 2026, not yet counted in the global status. On the globe, Krapp et al.'s maps are measured from their own present, which is pre-industrial, and Berkeley Earth's from 1850–1900: close, but not the same reference, so the colours may step slightly at 1850. Land has warmed faster than the sea (some 2 °C against about 1 °C in recent years), so the continents look warmer than the chart's line and the oceans cooler. Before 1850 the sea is left plain: Krapp et al.'s maps cover land only. Within about a degree of the reference the land is left uncoloured. High latitudes have warmed most: since 1951–1980 Arctic land some 2.5 °C, the tropics' about 1.2 °C.
certainty: Firm: CO₂ concentration, the ozone column and aragonite saturation, measured directly.
Modelled from observations: radiative forcing, freshwater disturbance, nutrient flows, forest cover.
Estimated within wide ranges: extinction rates and the energy taken from ecosystems.
Judged, with no numbers past the boundary: novel entities.
